The fingerboard has about eighteen or nineteen frets and the range is about two and two-thirds octaves. The requinto is smaller, with the middle strings in unison; its timbre is thinner and its pitch higher. The North American tiple has ten strings in groups of two, three, three and two with mixed octaves, and its deeper body gives it more volume.

The twelve-string Colombian type is regarded as that country's national instrument; it descends from the Renaissance Spanish vihuela, which Spanish conquerors brought to the New World in the sixteenth century, and took its present form at the end of the nineteenth century, with twelve strings in four groups of three and the middle string an octave below the outer ones. The Puerto Rican type can be traced to the eighteenth century; José Reyes Zamora holds that it descends from the Spanish guitarrillo, and the island has no single standard. The North American type was designed in 1919 by the Martin Guitar Company for the William J. Smith Company and was popular from the 1920s to the 1940s on the ukelele boom, used in jazz, blues and old-time country bands.

The Colombian tiple is common in traditional music such as the bambuco and the pasillo, as accompaniment or solo; Pacho Benavides has written works for tiple. The Puerto Rican tiple is one of the three string instruments of the jíbaro ensemble, played with the cuatro and the bordonua. The North American Martin tiple was used in jazz, blues and old-time country bands, and also served as a louder ukulele.

The Colombian twelve-string version traditionally pairs steel strings with copper strings, the copper ones mostly in the middle; abroad, brass- or bronze-wound steel strings are often used instead. The common five-string Puerto Rican type uses metal strings; the body may be guitar-shaped or carved from a single block of wood, and the head carries side or rear tuning machines. The Menorcan instrument has five nylon strings; the Dominican and Peruvian versions use steel strings. North American Martin models have mahogany, rosewood and spruce tops, some inlaid with mother-of-pearl. The materials of other parts are not stated.

The tiple is a fretted chordophone, H-S classification 321.322-5, of the guitar family; it usually has ten or twelve strings, built differently from region to region. The Colombian type has twelve strings in four groups of three, the outer strings tuned an octave high, and is used in traditional music such as the bambuco and the pasillo, as accompaniment or solo. The Puerto Rican type is smaller and is one of the string instruments of the jíbaro ensemble alongside the Cuatro and the Bordonua. The North American type has ten strings in four groups and was used in jazz, blues and old-time country bands.
